claim: Hitler's deputy flew solo to Scotland to find the first pilot over Everest.

knots.passage: In 1933, Lady Houston, a British millionaire, funded the Houston Everest Flight of 1933, which saw a formation of two aeroplanes led by the Marquess of Clydesdale fly over the Everest summit.
knots.hatnote: Twenty years before anyone stood on top, two planes flew over it.

knots.section: Air force career and flight over Everest
knots.passage: Flying in formation higher than any before; Lord Clydesdale, as he was then known, was chief pilot on the first flight over Mount Everest in 1933, flying a Westland PV-3 biplane. The extremity endured by the crews of these aeroplanes helped demonstrate the need for pressurised cabins in modern aircraft.
knots.hatnote: The lead pilot was a young Scottish aristocrat, later the Duke of Hamilton.

knots.passage: During World War II, Hamilton was involved in the 1941 aborted peace mission of Rudolf Hess, the Deputy Führer of the Nazi Party. After making a surprise landing in Scotland, Hess demanded to speak to Hamilton whom he believed was an opinion leader favouring peace with Germany.
knots.hatnote: Eight years later, the Everest pilot got a very unexpected visitor.

knots.passage: Haushofer spoke of his belief that it was possible to make contact with the king via either General Ian Hamilton or the Duke of Hamilton. Hess decided they should contact his fellow aviator the Duke of Hamilton. The two men were not acquainted with each other: Hamilton and Hess were both present at a banquet at the 1936 Summer Olympics, but they sat at different tables and never spoke.
knots.hatnote: Why Hamilton? Hess's adviser Karl Haushofer said the Duke could reach the King.

knots.passage: Shortly before midnight on 10 May 1941, Hess landed at Floors Farm, by Waterfoot, south of Glasgow, where he was discovered still struggling with his parachute by local ploughman David McLean. Identifying himself as "Hauptmann Alfred Horn", Hess said he had an important message for the Duke of Hamilton.
knots.hatnote: So Hess flew himself to Scotland, alone, and came down by parachute.

knots.passage: Hamilton had been on duty as wing commander at RAF Turnhouse near Edinburgh when Hess had arrived, and his station had been one of those that had tracked the progress of the flight. He arrived at Maryhill Barracks the next morning, and after examining Hess's effects, he met alone with the prisoner. Hess immediately admitted his true identity and outlined the reason for his flight.
knots.hatnote: Did Hess ever get to meet his Everest pilot?

payoff: Hess flew to Scotland to meet the Everest pilot, whose own RAF station tracked him in. They met only once Hess was a prisoner.
caveats: Both pages say Hess and Hamilton had never spoken; Hamilton was declared in Parliament innocent of any prior contact.
